caption:
The US Patent and Trademark Office has issued initial refusals on Anthropic's applications to register CLAUDE MYTHOS.
The examiner cited a likely confusion with three earlier MYTHOS trademarks owned by other companies.
The refusals are not final, and Anthropic can still respond.

Should AI companies have to pay up when someone else owns the name first?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Gerben IP
threads_text: The US trademark office just refused Anthropic's CLAUDE MYTHOS applications, because three other companies already filed MYTHOS marks. It is not final, but Anthropic may have to get all three to agree or pay for the name. Should Anthropic just rename it?

paragraphs.text: The US Patent and Trademark Office has issued initial refusals of two applications by Anthropic to register CLAUDE MYTHOS as a trademark, according to the trademark law firm Gerben IP and the legal news service Law360, which both reported the decision on October 22, 2026. The applications carry serial numbers 99872437 and 99872440.

Law360 reported that the office preliminarily found the term would likely be confused with an existing registration. Gerben IP wrote that the examiner refused registration under Section 2(d) of the Trademark Act, the provision that covers a likelihood of confusion with marks that were filed or registered earlier.

According to Gerben IP, the examiner pointed to three earlier MYTHOS filings. One covers software for managing university endowment processes and donors. A second covers software for organizing, managing and sharing documents and content. The third covers artificial intelligence software for storing, managing and searching content created by users.

Gerben IP noted that none of the three companies behind those marks appears to compete directly with Anthropic. The firm explained that the office judges confusion from how goods and services are described in the filings, not from how the businesses compete in practice, so broad descriptions in an earlier application can block a later one even when the products differ.

The refusals are not final. Gerben IP listed several routes open to Anthropic: amending the descriptions of goods and services in its applications to set them apart from the earlier marks, arguing that consumers would not be confused, or reaching consent agreements with the owners of the earlier MYTHOS marks, which the office may accept. The firm added that Anthropic could also offer payment in exchange for consent or to acquire the rights outright.

Josh Gerben, who wrote the analysis, said that because the earlier filings are broad, Anthropic could face a significant challenge overcoming the refusals with legal arguments alone. He added that getting consent from every relevant owner would likely be difficult, since those companies filed first and hold potential leverage. He also pointed out that more than 500,000 new trademark applications are filed in the United States each year, leaving the register crowded, especially in software.
Why the Mythos name carries weight

Claude Mythos is the name of Anthropic's most powerful family of models. The company first disclosed Mythos on April 7, 2026, and chose not to release it to the public because of its ability to find software vulnerabilities, giving access instead to more than 40 companies through a program called Project Glasswing. Anthropic released Claude Mythos 5 as a preview through that program on June 9, 2026.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the refusal is an early procedural step rather than a ruling that Anthropic must drop the name, and companies often resolve this kind of office action through narrower descriptions or private agreements. The case does show how crowded short, evocative words have become in software, and how a large AI company can end up negotiating with much smaller firms that simply filed first.

The next step to watch is Anthropic's formal response to the office actions, and whether it narrows its applications, signs consent agreements with the three earlier MYTHOS owners, or adjusts how it brands the model.
